scenes.heading: Nucleic acids and proteins
scenes.sub: The instructions, and the molecules that carry them out
scenes.say: Every cell runs on two families of big molecules. Nucleic acids store and carry instructions. Proteins carry them out. So how does a DNA sequence become a protein?

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: The master recipe book stays in the office; cooks use a photocopy
scenes.science: DNA stays in the nucleus; mRNA is a working copy for the ribosome
scenes.breaks: a photocopy is identical, but mRNA is complementary to the template strand and uses uracil and ribose.
scenes.say: Think of a canteen's master recipe book that never leaves the office. That's DNA: double-stranded, stable and kept safe. When cooks need one recipe, they get a photocopy. That's mRNA: a single-stranded, short-lived copy of one gene that goes to the ribosome, the kitchen bench.

scenes.heading: DNA vs RNA
scenes.say: Both are made of nucleotides: a phosphate, a sugar and a base. DNA is a double helix with deoxyribose and the bases A, T, G and C. RNA is usually single-stranded, has ribose, and uses uracil instead of thymine.

scenes.heading: Base pairing
points: A pairs with T; G pairs with C
scenes.say: Apple in the tree, car in the garage: A pairs with T, and C pairs with G. G and C share three hydrogen bonds, A and T share two. The two strands are antiparallel.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: Double-stranded DNA contains 18% adenine. What are the percentages of the other bases?
lines: A pairs with T, so T = 18%
scenes.say: If DNA has eighteen percent adenine, it must have eighteen percent thymine. That's thirty-six percent together, leaving sixty-four percent for G and C. Split it evenly: thirty-two percent each.
scenes.caption: If DNA has 18% adenine, it must have 18% thymine. That's 36% together, leaving 64% for G and C. Split it evenly: 32% each.

scenes.heading: Building polymers
points: n amino acids: n − 1 peptide bonds
scenes.say: Both nucleic acids and proteins are built by condensation polymerisation. Each new bond releases a water molecule. Nucleotides are joined by phosphodiester bonds, and amino acids by peptide bonds. Like fence posts and rails, a chain of n amino acids has n minus one peptide bonds.

scenes.heading: The genetic code
points: 61 code for amino acids; 3 are stop codons
scenes.say: The genetic code is read in triplets. Four bases, three at a time, gives sixty-four codons. Sixty-one code for amino acids and three are stop codons. A U G is the start. The code is degenerate, meaning several codons can code for one amino acid. It's also universal and non-overlapping.
scenes.caption: The genetic code is read in triplets. Four bases, three at a time, gives 64 codons. 61 code for amino acids and 3 are stop codons. AUG is the start. The code is degenerate, meaning several codons can code for one amino acid. It's also universal and non-overlapping.

points: DNA: double helix, A–T and G–C
RNA: single strand, ribose and uracil
scenes.say: Quick recap. DNA is a double helix with A T and G C pairs. RNA uses ribose and uracil. Condensation joins monomers. And the triplet code has sixty-four codons. Now try the practice questions!
